what: A rate limiter counts how many requests each caller makes in a time window and turns away the extras with HTTP 429, so one busy client cannot crowd out everyone else.
like: Like a theme park ride that lets 20 people on every few minutes: the queue moves steadily and the ride never gets overloaded.
why: Protects your servers and database from spikes, bugs and abuse
Shares capacity fairly between users, API keys or tenants
Tells clients clearly when to slow down and when to try again

steps.d: The limiter builds a key from who is calling and which rule applies, such as user:42:per-minute. Each key gets its own count.
One Lua script in Redis reads the count, decides and writes back in a single atomic step, so two requests can never both take the last slot.
Token bucket: tokens refill at a steady rate up to a cap, and each request spends one. The cap is the burst you allow; an empty bucket means no.
The request goes to your API. Replies can carry a RateLimit header telling the client how much quota is left and when the window resets.
The limiter replies 429 Too Many Requests, ideally with Retry-After in seconds. Good clients wait, then retry with exponential backoff plus random jitter.
Every gateway uses the same Redis keys, so the limit holds across the whole fleet. Graph allowed versus limited to tune rules safely.

choices.d: Token bucket allows short bursts with a steady average. Leaky bucket gives a smooth, no-burst flow. Sliding window counter is a cheap, accurate default. Fixed window is simplest but bursts at edges.
Per API key or user is fairest. Per IP works for logged-out traffic. Add per-endpoint rules for expensive calls, and a global cap to protect the whole service.
Pick the steady rate and how big a burst is fine, e.g. 10 per second with a bucket of 50. Dark launch first: log who would be limited before you enforce.
At the edge or API gateway to stop traffic early, or inside the service for limits that need business context. Many systems use both.
Fail open (allow, maybe with a local in-memory limit) to keep serving, or fail closed (deny) for sensitive actions like logins. Decide up front.

instead.why: Built-in throttling and quotas per key, with no limiter code to write
Accept every request and work through the backlog at your own pace
Protects you from a slow downstream service rather than from noisy callers

breaks.d: A fixed window resets on the minute, so a client can use a full quota just before and again just after.
breaks.see: Traffic spikes at the start of every window, up to twice the limit
breaks.fix: Sliding window counter or token bucket

breaks.d: Read then write as separate calls, so two servers both see room and both allow.
breaks.see: More requests get through than the limit under heavy load
breaks.fix: One atomic Lua script (or INCR) per check in Redis

breaks.d: Limited clients retry at once and keep the pressure on.
breaks.see: 429 rate stays high, with the same clients retrying in tight loops
breaks.fix: Send Retry-After; clients back off exponentially with jitter

breaks.d: A real spike, like a flash sale, hits limits sized for normal days.
breaks.see: 429s for real customers and a dip in successful orders
breaks.fix: Dark launch rules, limit per customer, raise limits before big events

say: I'll rate limit at the API gateway per API key with a token bucket, so short bursts are fine but the average rate is capped.
Counters live in Redis and each check is one Lua script, so the limit is exact across every gateway node.
Over the limit we return 429 with Retry-After, and our clients back off with jitter.
If Redis is unreachable we fail open with a small local limit, because blocking every user is worse than letting a few extra requests through.

followups.a: Token bucket lets bursts through up to the bucket size, then holds the average rate. Leaky bucket drains at a fixed rate, so output stays smooth with no bursts. As meters they are mirror images; the difference is mainly burst behaviour.

followups.q: How do you make it work across 50 servers?
followups.a: Keep the counters in a shared store like Redis and do each check atomically in one round trip with a Lua script. In Redis Cluster, use hash tags so all keys for one limit land in the same slot.

followups.q: Why not store every request timestamp?
followups.a: A sliding window log is exact but memory grows with traffic, up to one entry per request per client. A sliding window counter keeps two numbers and blends them, which Cloudflare found nearly as accurate.

followups.q: What should a client do when it gets 429?
followups.a: Wait at least the Retry-After time if given, then retry with exponential backoff plus random jitter so clients don't all return at once. Better still, limit itself on the client side.

today: The IETF RateLimit header fields draft (version 11, May 2026) is still an Internet-Draft, not yet an RFC; it defines RateLimit-Policy and RateLimit headers as one shared format instead of the many X-RateLimit-* variants.

check.q: Your API should allow short bursts but cap the average rate. Which algorithm?
check.why: Saved-up tokens allow a burst up to the bucket size, while the refill rate sets the average.

check.q: Which status code means 'you sent too many requests'?
check.why: 429 Too Many Requests is the rate limit code; a Retry-After header can say when to try again.

check.q: Two gateways share one Redis limit. How do you stop both taking the last slot?
check.a: Check and update in one atomic Lua script
d: GET the count, then SET it
Give each gateway half the limit
check.why: Redis runs a script without interleaving other commands, so the read-decide-write cannot race.

check.q: What is the main weakness of a fixed window counter?
check.a: Bursts of up to 2x the limit at window edges
d: It needs one key per request
check.why: A client can spend a full quota at the end of one window and again at the start of the next.
